content: Traditional herbal medicines can lead to falsely elevated APRI scores, which may misrepresent the severity of liver disease. Hepatitis flares, acute hepatitis, congestive heart failure, or even a recent meal can also result in elevated liver stiffness measurements when assessed using elastography techniques. The diagnostic accuracy of the APRI score has not been comprehensively evaluated in the context of various comorbidities. Furthermore, there is a lack of specific evaluation of non-invasive tests (NITs), including APRI, in populations such as children or individuals from sub-Saharan Africa. Transient elastography (FibroScan) has several limitations. It relies on a single cut-off value, which may lead to overestimation of its sensitivity and specificity across different stages of fibrosis. There are no universally validated cut-off values for specific fibrosis stages. Its accuracy is reduced in obese individuals, in the presence of moderate to severe necroinflammation, right-sided heart failure, or following food intake. Additionally, transient elastography cannot be performed in patients with ascites and is contraindicated in cases where ALT levels fluctuate significantly, as seen in chronic hepatitis B, necessitating longitudinal monitoring to identify trends. The upper limits of normal ALT levels are defined as less than 30 U/L for men and 19 U/L for women, though local laboratory reference ranges should be applied. Persistently abnormal or normal ALT levels are defined as three measurements above or below the upper limit of normal, taken at unspecified intervals over a 6–12-month period or at predefined intervals over a 12-month period. In pregnant women, data on the use of transient elastography are limited, and specialized probes are required for children. For individuals co-infected with HBV and HIV, the performance of NITs is unlikely to differ significantly from those with HBV mono-infection, although data are limited. From a patient perspective, the APRI test is considered acceptable due to its simplicity, requiring only routine blood tests and phlebotomy, which can be performed by untrained staff. Similarly, transient elastography is non-invasive, quick (less than 10 minutes), and can be conducted in outpatient or community settings with minimal training required for healthcare staff. However, the use of transient elastography is limited by the high cost of equipment, the need for regular maintenance and recalibration, and the requirement for trained operators. The lack of extensively validated cut-off values for specific fibrosis stages further complicates its use. The cost of acquiring and maintaining a FibroScan machine is substantial, with prices ranging from $34,000 to $50,000 and annual maintenance costs of $8,500. Despite minimal consumable costs, the overall expense makes it less feasible in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). In contrast, blood-based NITs like APRI are more cost-effective and widely available, even in LMICs, with each test costing only a few dollars. The interpretation of APRI results, particularly with a high cut-off of >2 for diagnosing cirrhosis in adults, is relatively straightforward. FibroScan requires specialized probes for children and individuals with a body mass index (BMI) >30 kg/m². These factors, along with the high cost and maintenance requirements, make transient elastography and FibroTest less feasible in most LMICs. The WHO guidelines recommend prioritizing treatment for all adults, adolescents, and children with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) who have clinical evidence of compensated or decompensated cirrhosis, regardless of ALT levels, HBeAg status, or HBV DNA levels. Treatment is also recommended for adults with CHB who are over 30 years old, have persistently abnormal ALT levels, and evidence of high-level HBV replication (HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL), even in the absence of cirrhosis. In settings where HBV DNA testing is unavailable, treatment may be considered based on persistently abnormal ALT levels alone. Antiviral therapy is not recommended for individuals without cirrhosis, with persistently normal ALT levels, and low levels of HBV replication (HBV DNA <2,000 IU/mL), regardless of HBeAg status or age. Continued monitoring is essential for all individuals with CHB, particularly those who do not currently meet treatment criteria, to determine if antiviral therapy may be indicated in the future. The initial assessment of individuals with CHB should include a thorough history, physical examination, and laboratory tests to evaluate liver disease severity, including ALT, AST, ALP, total bilirubin, platelet count, and synthetic liver function (serum albumin and prothrombin time/INR). Assessment of viral replication through HBV DNA quantification and HBeAg/anti-HBe serostatus is also critical. Screening for comorbidities, such as HIV, HCV, HDV co-infections, metabolic disorders, and alcohol-related liver disease, is necessary. All individuals with cirrhosis should be screened for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Patients should receive counseling on lifestyle modifications, including alcohol reduction, diet, and physical activity, as well as the importance of adherence to long-term treatment to prevent disease progression and drug resistance.
